title: Extract a list of unique departments from the employee list.
shortTitle: Extract a list of unique departments from the employee list

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This combines `map` to project the department field with `distinct()` to remove duplicates, producing a stream of unique department names. `distinct()` uses `equals` and `hashCode` to decide uniqueness and is a stateful intermediate operation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The HR manager at the National Bank of India wants the list of departments that actually exist, each named once, to plan an org chart. Many employees share a department, so she writes down each department the first time she sees it and ignores repeats. `map` plus `distinct` is exactly that — pull the department, then keep only the first of each.

**One line to remember:** `map` to the field, then `distinct()` to drop repeats, giving each unique value once.

sections.s2_technical:
First you project each employee to its department with `map(Employee::getDepartment)`, turning the stream of employees into a stream of department strings. That stream will contain repeats because many employees share a department. The `distinct()` intermediate operation then removes duplicates, keeping only the first occurrence of each value in encounter order.

`distinct()` decides whether two elements are the same by calling `equals` and using `hashCode`. For strings this works out of the box because String has well-defined equals and hashCode. If you were distinct-ing custom objects you would have to override both methods correctly, otherwise distinct would treat every object as unique by identity and remove nothing.

`distinct()` is stateful, meaning it must remember the values it has already seen, typically in an internal set. On a sequential stream it preserves encounter order. On a parallel stream maintaining order is more expensive, so if order does not matter you can call `unordered()` to let the engine drop the ordering constraint and run faster.

A senior nuance: if you want the result as a set rather than a list, `collect(Collectors.toSet())` gives uniqueness for free without a separate distinct, because a set inherently rejects duplicates. The choice between distinct-then-toList and toSet depends on whether you need to preserve encounter order (use distinct and a list) or only need uniqueness (a set is simpler).
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is drawing up a new organisational chart and needs the definitive list of departments that currently exist, each listed exactly once. The employee list has hundreds of people and the same department name repeats for everyone in it, so simply listing departments per employee would be full of duplicates. This is exactly how map plus distinct works — each employee is projected to its department, then duplicates are removed so each department appears a single time.

The code defines an `Employee` with name and department. An `OrgChartService` exposes `uniqueDepartments(List<Employee>)` using map then distinct. The runnable `Main` feeds employees with repeated departments and logs the unique list.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (IT), Priya (Sales), Amit (IT), Neha (HR), Karan (Sales).

Step 1: The stream opens over five employees.

Step 2: map projects each to its department, producing the stream IT, Sales, IT, HR, Sales — which clearly has repeats.

Step 3: distinct sees IT first and keeps it, recording IT in its internal seen-set.

Step 4: distinct sees Sales, not seen before, keeps it.

Step 5: distinct sees IT again, already in the seen-set, drops it.

Step 6: distinct sees HR, new, keeps it. Then sees Sales again, already seen, drops it.

Step 7: `collect` gathers the unique departments IT, Sales, HR in encounter order.

```
Oct 30, 2026 11:35:07 AM com.bank.orgchart.service.OrgChartService uniqueDepartments
INFO: Deriving unique departments from 5 employees
Oct 30, 2026 11:35:07 AM com.bank.orgchart.Main lambda$main$0
INFO: Unique departments: [IT, Sales, HR]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [Rajesh IT, Priya Sales, Amit IT, Neha HR, Karan Sales]
    │
    ▼
  map(getDepartment)  → [IT, Sales, IT, HR, Sales]  (has repeats)
    │
    ▼
  distinct()  (seen-set, equals/hashCode)
    ├─ IT     → new  → keep
    ├─ Sales  → new  → keep
    ├─ IT     → seen → drop
    ├─ HR     → new  → keep
    └─ Sales  → seen → drop
    │
    ▼
  collect(toList())  →  [IT, Sales, HR]  (encounter order preserved)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To get the unique values of a field I combine two operations: I map each object to the field I care about, then I call distinct to remove the duplicates. For departments I mapped every employee to its department string, which produces a stream full of repeats because many people share a department, and then distinct kept only the first occurrence of each, giving me each department exactly once in the order it first appeared.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was building the definitive department list for a new org chart. The employee list had hundreds of people with the same department names repeating, so I projected to the department and applied distinct to collapse the repeats into a clean list.

A senior point I always add is how distinct decides uniqueness: it relies on the equals and hashCode methods. For strings this just works because String defines both correctly, but if I were distinct-ing custom objects I would have to override equals and hashCode properly, otherwise distinct would compare by identity and remove nothing. I also mention that distinct is stateful — it keeps an internal set of what it has seen — and preserves encounter order on a sequential stream, whereas on a parallel stream dropping the ordering constraint can be faster. If I only need uniqueness and do not care about order, collecting straight into a set is a simpler alternative that gives uniqueness for free.
